# Indonesia

Wealth gradients in fertility and mortality: the values for an OG-Core calibration, followed by the estimates they are based on. Terms are defined in the [glossary](../glossary.md).

## Values for OG-Core

| OG-Core input | Wealth gradient | Source |
|---|---|---|
| `fert_gradient` | −0.38, by age as below | DHS 2017, TFR, plus [age offsets](../methods/fertility-by-age.md) |
| `infmort_gradient` | −0.73 | DHS 2017, infant mortality rate |
| `mort_gradient` | −1.16 (95% prediction interval −1.87 to −0.45) | [general gradient](../methods/general-gradient.md) at GDP per capita (PPP, constant 2021 international $) of $14,471 (2024) |
| `imm_pctiles` | not provided | — |

Values are [wealth gradients](../glossary.md#wealth-gradient). Before they are passed to OG-Core, each is divided by 100 × (1 − p), where p is OG-Core's rate at that age ([details](../methods/ogcore-units.md)).

**Fertility gradient by age of mother** (`fert_gradient`; ages below 15 use the 15–19 value, ages 50 and above the 45–49 value):

| 15–19 | 20–24 | 25–29 | 30–34 | 35–39 | 40–44 | 45–49 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| −1.16 | −0.48 | −0.18 | −0.06 | −0.29 | −0.78 | −1.37 |

**Adult and child mortality gradient by age** (`mort_gradient`; ages 15–59: the 45q15 gradient above plus the pooled offset for each band ([age pattern](../methods/general-gradient.md#age-pattern)); ages 5–14 use the 15–29 value; ages 60–74 fall in a straight line from the 45–59 value to 0 at age 75; ages 75 and above, and OG-Core's final age, use 0):

| 1–4 | 5–14 | 15–29 | 30–44 | 45–59 | 60–74 | 75+ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| pending | −1.54 | −1.54 | −1.31 | −0.97 | −0.97 at 60, falling to 0 at 75 | 0 |

Ages 1–4 await a decision on the method (the child-mortality gradient at ages 1–4; [ROADMAP](../../ROADMAP.md) item A3). Infant mortality (age 0) is `infmort_gradient`, above.

## Estimates

### Household surveys

Latest Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) or Multiple Indicator Cluster Survey (MICS) with a complete wealth-quintile breakdown, for each indicator ([`gradient_library_latest.csv`](../../data/gradient_library_latest.csv); earlier surveys in `gradient_library.csv`).

| Indicator | Survey | Lowest | Second | Middle | Fourth | Highest | Low/high ratio | Gradient |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Total fertility rate (births per woman) | DHS 2017 | 2.9 | 2.6 | 2.3 | 2.3 | 2.1 | 1.38 | −0.38 |
| Infant mortality rate (per 1,000 live births) | DHS 2017 | 40 | 26 | 23 | 24 | 20 | 2.00 | −0.73 |
| Under-five mortality rate (per 1,000 live births) | DHS 2017 | 52 | 33 | 29 | 31 | 24 | 2.17 | −0.80 |

## Notes

- No census or survey with a household-deaths module is available (the country's DHS surveys have no module on deaths of household members at all ages), so adult mortality uses the general gradient (value in the table above). Fertility and infant mortality come from the 2017 IDHS.
- Cross-check: a cohort study of the Indonesia Family Life Survey (Sudharsanan 2019, J Gerontol B 74(3), doi:10.1093/geronb/gbx061; adults aged 30–80 in 2007, followed to 2014–15, 1,443 deaths) reports odds ratios of death by quartile of a DHS-type asset index. Fitted across the quartile midpoints, they imply wealth gradients of −0.61 (urban women), −0.30 (urban men), +0.06 (rural women) and −0.45 (rural men), mean −0.32. These are for ages 30–80, where gradients are weaker than in 45q15 (see the age offsets of the general gradient), and each rests on a few hundred deaths; they are consistent with the general gradient but too imprecise to replace it. By a rough calculation from the sample size and national mortality, the survey's own microdata would hold fewer than the 900 deaths at ages 15–59 needed for a publishable estimate.
- The wealth gradient in the total fertility rate is modest, while the gradient in adolescent fertility (ages 15–19) is among the steepest in the library: the differential is concentrated in the timing of births.
